finding: In LUCI, cotton-fiberglass (SIBAL) fabric flames went out about 45 s later in simulated lunar gravity than in the 1-g comparison burn.
quote: 1-g extinction happens ~ 45 seconds sooner than partial-g extinction

finding: LUCI showed that material flammability testing at partial gravity is feasible on a spinning suborbital vehicle (Blue Origin New Shepard).
quote: The LUCI scientific objectives were achieved. Material flammability testing at partial-g is feasible using a spinning vehicle.

finding: On LUCI's spinning rocket, the Coriolis force pulled the PMMA flame away from the fuel axis, which was aligned with the centrifugal acceleration.
quote: The one on the right demonstrates how the Coriolis force pulls the flame away from the axis of the fuel, which is aligned with the direction of the centrifugal acceleration.

finding: A 4-mm PMMA rod burning upward in air in simulated lunar gravity grew until its flame engulfed the entire rod.
quote: PMMA rod burning upward in air in Lunar-g, 30 s after ignition. The flame eventually grows to engulf the entire rod.

finding: Drop-tower centrifuge data show the oxygen level at which materials self-extinguish (MOC) can be lower at lunar gravity than at zero or Martian gravity.
quote: Lunar-g MOC can be lower than either zero- or Martian-g levels

finding: In partial-gravity drop-tower tests, Nomex, Mylar and Ultem flames all propagated at the oxygen level where they self-extinguish in normal gravity.
quote: Partial-g flames propagated at the normal-g MOC for all materials (charring and non-charring)

finding: Theory and experiments indicate oxygen flammability limits at lunar gravity are lower than those measured at 1 g.
quote: Theory and experimental results indicate that oxygen flammability limits in lunar-g are lower than those measured in 1-g

finding: Turning off cabin ventilation to starve a fire is not effective at lunar gravity, because buoyancy still drives flow.
quote: Turning the ECLSS flow off to extinguish a fire in lunar-g is not effective because the reduced gravity will still induce buoyant flow velocities

finding: In partial gravity, smoke transport for fire detection involves a competition between smoke production rate, buoyancy and ventilation air circulation.
quote: In partial-g, there will be a competition between rate of smoke production, buoyancy, and ECLSS air circulation

finding: Models show that in zero gravity with forced ventilation, the spacecraft volume must reach alarm-level smoke before a detector alarm sounds.
quote: Modeling has shown that in zero-g with forced convection, the spacecraft volume must reach the alarm level before an alarm will sound

finding: On ISS, flames over 12.7-mm PMMA rods in microgravity were weaker but still propagated, and at lower oxygen than in 1 g.
quote: The microgravity flame is weaker but can still propagate and at lower %O2 than in 1-g

finding: Normal-gravity MOC data show raising oxygen concentration affects flammability much more than raising pressure, similarly across materials.
quote: The nearly vertical lines for the pressure vs. MOC show that increasing oxygen has a significantly greater effect than increasing pressure

finding: SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric burns downward in air at lunar gravity (centrifuge and parabolic tests), yet extinguishes immediately after ignition at Earth gravity.
quote: SIBAL fabric has been found to only burn downward in air in lunar gravity (via Lunar gravity centrifuge and parabolic flight) where on Earth’s gravity it extinguishes immediately after ignition.

finding: FM2 drop-tower centrifuge tests (5.18 s) give increasing evidence that materials have lower oxygen flammability limits at lunar than at Earth gravity.
quote: Provides Increasing evidence that materials have lower oxygen limits of flammability in Lunar gravity than in Earth gravity according to the 5.18 second tests using the zero-gravity drop facility.

finding: In ground (1-g) tests, SIBAL fabric burned downward with a bright flame in 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi.
quote: A bright flame burns SIBAL fuel downwards in 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi

finding: Nomex HT90-40 fabric needed more oxygen to burn at lunar gravity (~29%) and 0 g (~38%) than at 1 g (~23%).
quote: Limiting oxygen concentrations (LOC): o 1G ~23% Oxygen o Lunar-G ~29% Oxygen o 0G ~38% Oxygen

finding: In 1-g flow-tunnel tests, imposed flow had negligible effect on Nomex flame length and spread, likely because buoyancy outweighed the imposed flow.
quote: Flow rate has negligible effect on flame length and flame spread over the tested range. Likely due to the buoyant force outweighing the imposed flow

finding: In 1-g flow-tunnel tests of Nomex HT90-40 at 8.2 psi, higher oxygen concentration increased flame length and tip spread rate.
quote: Oxygen concentration is observed to increase flame length and tip spread rate.

finding: Martian-gravity drop-tower tests suggest a gravity level below Earth's exists at which materials burn more readily than on Earth.
quote: the data presented in this paper for Martian gravity suggest that there is a gravity level below Earth’s at which materials burn more readily than on Earth.

finding: For Mylar, Ultem and Nomex, 1-g flammability limits were generally not conservative: reduced-gravity limits were up to 5.75% oxygen lower.
quote: As shown in Fig. 6 and Table I, the 1g flammability limits are generally not conservative for these materials as evidenced by the negative ∆O2%, by up to -5.75% oxygen.

finding: For charring fuels (Nomex, Ultem), the oxygen margin of safety at lunar gravity was about 2.5% oxygen below 1 g.
quote: In Lunar gravity, the oxygen margin of safety for these charring fuels is ~ 2.5% lower than 1g.

finding: For non-charring Mylar, the lack of gravity-driven dripping keeps molten fuel in the flame zone, giving a 4-5% oxygen negative safety margin.
quote: the absence of gravitational-induced dripping keeps heated molten fuel in the flame zone rather than removing it, and the result is a significantly negative oxygen margin of safety (~4-5%) in Martian, Lunar, and 0g.

finding: For charring Nomex and Ultem, the oxygen safety margin at 0 g (30 cm/s concurrent flow) was close to zero relative to 1 g.
quote: For these charring materials, the oxygen margin of safety in 0g is very close to zero, indicating that any reduced charring for 0g may be offset by less heat release in the reduced convective environment.

finding: Consistently negative safety margins suggest 1-g flammability screening may not be conservative: some materials rated safe for space may actually be flammable.
quote: normal gravity material flammability screening tests may not be conservative and some materials tested to be safe for use in space may actually be flammable.

finding: Mylar's limiting oxygen versus gravity level is bounded by two U-shaped curves: flames survive only within a range of g-levels.
quote: The two u-shaped curves are presumed to bound the flammability boundary of this material.

finding: In low gravity, anything that restricts free oxygen flow past a burning sample, such as edge curling or swelling, reduces its flammability.
quote: Since oxygen transport is critical to low gravity flames, anything that reduces the free flow of oxygen past the sample will reduce the material’s flammability.

finding: In KC-135 partial-gravity flights, upward flame spread rate over thin tissue varied linearly with gravity level for all pressures and widths tested.
quote: The upward burning spread rate varied linearly with gravity level for all pressure environments and sample widths tested

finding: Downward flame spread rate over thin tissue was non-monotonic with gravity, peaking near Martian gravity (0.38 g) in 27.6 kPa air.
quote: The downward spread rate is non-monotonic and peaks near the Martian gravity levels of 0.38 g/gEarth.

finding: The downward-spread flammability boundary versus gravity is U-shaped: extinction from short residence time at high g and radiative loss at low g.
quote: The downward spreading boundary is U-shaped showing the dual extinction limits (insufficient residence time in high g, radiative loss in low g) now predicted by several diffusion flame models.

finding: In partial-gravity flights, upward-spreading flames over thin tissue had a wider flammable domain than downward-spreading flames.
quote: The upward spreading case has a wider flammable domain that the downward case.

finding: A 3-D model of the limiting oxygen index (LOI) apparatus predicted lower limiting oxygen at zero gravity than at normal gravity.
quote: The LOI at normal gravity are higher than those at zero gravity for the range of forced velocity computed.

finding: The same model predicts the zero-gravity LOI for cotton-fiberglass is non-monotonic in forced flow, with a minimum around 5 cm/s.
quote: the LOI at zero gravity is non-monotonic and has a minimum around 5 cm/s

finding: Theory comparing spread directions finds the lowest flammable oxygen percentage always occurs in concurrent (wind-aided) flow, not opposed flow.
quote: However, the lowest flammable oxygen percentage is always in the concurrent flow case.

finding: Earlier parabolic-flight tests of downward burning found faster flame spread and lower limiting oxygen as gravity was reduced below Earth gravity.
quote: These results indicated increases in flame spread rates and enhanced flammability (lower limiting atmospheric oxygen content) as gravity levels were reduced from normal Earth gravity

finding: Theory and experiments show some materials that will not burn at 1 g will burn at 0 g with low-speed flow, or at lunar gravity.
quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).

finding: SIBAL fabric 2.2 cm wide supports both concurrent and opposed-flow spread in microgravity, but downward (opposed) spread cannot be achieved on Earth.
quote: In microgravity, both concurrent and opposed-flow flame spread are possible, but on Earth, downward flame spread (opposed flow) cannot be achieved. This demonstrates enhanced flammability in microgravity, and suggests similar behavior at partial gravity.

finding: A model shows the oxygen concentration needed for flammability reaches its minimum near lunar gravity.
quote: Oxygen concentration for flammability reaches a minimum value in the vicinity of g = gMoon (left; model)

finding: A crew-cabin fire model calibrated on large-scale exploration-atmosphere tests predicted substantially higher cabin air temperatures at lunar gravity than at 1 g.
quote: Air temperature in the lunar-g simulation was substantially higher than in 1-g showing buoyant transport significantly affects habitability

finding: A material that passes NASA's upward Test 1 would most likely not burn in quiescent (no-flow) microgravity.
quote: A material that passes this test would most likely not burn in a quiescent microgravity environment

finding: For some materials the most flammable condition is at very low flow velocities, below those produced by upward burning in normal gravity.
quote: The most flammable condition for some materials is at very low velocities, below those for upward spread in normal gravity

label: Rotating sounding rocket (LUCI)
text: Blue Origin's New Shepard sounding rocket can produce lunar gravity for burn tests by spinning (centrifugal acceleration).
quote: Blue Origin New Shepard sounding rocket yields Lunar gravity by using centrifugal acceleration.

label: LUCI hypothesis
text: NASA's LUCI team hypothesised that some materials are more flammable in partial gravity than on Earth, with implications for NASA's 1-g screening test.
quote: Hypothesis: some materials burning in partial-g are more flammable than on Earth. This has important implications for the current 1-g material screening method used by NASA.

label: LUCI
text: LUCI burned a cotton-fiberglass fabric and a 4-mm acrylic (PMMA) rod together in air at normal pressure in simulated lunar gravity.
quote: Two samples are burned simultaneously in air at normal pressure: Cotton-fiberglass composite fabric sheet and a 4-mm diameter rod of acrylic plastic (polymethyl methacrylate).

label: LUCI
text: After launch-provider delays, LUCI finally launched on 4 February 2025.
quote: Initial Planned launch was Spring 2023, Launch provider delay initially delayed launch into late Summer early Fall 2024, until it finally launched Feb 4 2025

label: FM2
text: FM2 will perform burn tests on the lunar surface; as of December 2025 it was planned to launch in late 2026.
quote: performing burn tests on the Lunar surface in the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment which is planned to launch in late 2026

label: FM2
text: FM2 will fly on an uncrewed SpaceX Human Lander System test flight.
quote: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment which will fly on a SpaceX Human Lander System unmanned test flight.

label: 0 g vs lunar g
text: Configurations that cannot support a flame in low gravity could support one at lunar gravity.
quote: Configurations that will not support a flame in low-gravity could support a flame in lunar-gravity

label: Caveat: material-dependent
text: How a material's self-extinguishing oxygen level varies with gravity depends on the material.
quote: Variation of MOC with gravity level is dependent on the material

label: No partial-g acceptance criterion
text: NASA still needs work to establish a partial-gravity flammability acceptance criterion.
quote: Additional work is needed to establish a partial gravity flammability acceptance criterion

label: Tiny lunar data set
text: Because partial-gravity test platforms are scarce, the data set of lunar flammability tests is very small.
quote: Owing to lack of access to partial gravity test platforms, the data set of lunar flammability tests is very small

label: NASA's lunar-g test plan
text: NASA planned to quantify the lunar oxygen-limit shift with models, low-gravity aircraft, a drop-tower centrifuge and a rotating suborbital capsule, anchored by a lunar lander test.
quote: We are developing a plan to quantify the magnitude of ∆%O2 using a combination of modeling, low-gravity aircraft, drop tower centrifuge, and rotating capsule in a sub-orbital flight to be anchored by a lunar lander test

label: Lunar lander (CLPS)
text: A lunar-lander (CLPS) flammability experiment provides 'lunar truth', but its tests are very limited in size and number.
quote: Provides a “Lunar truth” but tests are very limited in size and number

label: Parabolic aircraft
text: Parabolic aircraft give about 20 s of direct partial-gravity burning.
quote: Parabolic Aircraft 20 sec Direct partial-g burn

label: Drop-tower centrifuge
text: A centrifuge rig in NASA Glenn's Zero Gravity Facility drop tower gives 5 s of direct partial-gravity burning to measure flammability limits.
quote: ZGF Centrifuge Rig 5 sec Direct partial-g burn – flammability limits

label: EVA suit
text: US EVA suits used on ISS operate at 4.3 psia with 100% oxygen by volume.
quote: EVA suit: 4.3 psia, 100% O2 by volume (U.S. suits on ISS)

label: Blow-off at 1 g and lunar g
text: At both 1 g and lunar gravity, flame extinction near the limit is by blow-off.
quote: In both 1-g and lunar conditions, extinction is by blow-off

label: Lunar 'goldilocks zone'
text: Lunar gravity widens flammability limits for some materials: a 'goldilocks zone' with less convective heat loss but enough buoyant flow to resupply oxygen.
quote: Lunar gravity has been found to increase the limits of flammability for some materials compared to Earth gravity, presenting a goldilocks zone of reduced convective heat loss, while generating enough buoyant flow to replenish fresh oxygen into the flame zone.

label: HLS and lunar rover atmospheres
text: FM2 can replicate the two atmospheres of immediate interest to NASA's Human Lander System and lunar rover: 21% O2 at 14.7 psia and 34% O2 at 8.2 psia.
quote: specifically 21% oxygen at 14.7 psia, and 34% oxygen at 8.2 psia, which are of immediate interest to the Human Lander System (HLS) and Lunar Rover.

label: FM2
text: FM2 will provide the reference for how materials burn under long-term lunar gravity, to help mitigate fire risk for surface missions.
quote: It will provide the reference for how materials burn under the effect of long term Lunar gravity to help understand and mitigate the risk for future surface exploration missions.

label: Counterexample: Nomex
text: Counterexample: Nomex HT90-40 behaved differently from other materials; gravity strongly affected its flammability.
quote: Gravity has significant effects on the material’s flammability. o Nomex HT90-40® behaves differently than other materials when burned.

label: Earth tests can mislead
text: Materials that are not flammable on Earth can become flammable when oxygen level, cabin pressure or gravity change.
quote: Materials that are not flammable on Earth can become flammable when these conditions change.

label: FM2
text: FM2's planned lunar fire experiments will determine the limiting oxygen concentration of a flight-relevant material (Synergy Pro).
quote: Planned fire experiments on the moon. Currently scheduled in the next few years. Will determine limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) for a flight-relevant material (Synergy Pro).

label: Flammability map
text: The FM2 team's flammability map bounds a flammable region by blow-off extinction and radiative extinction against flow velocity or gravity level.
quote: Flow Velocity (or Gravity Level) Flammable Region Blow-off Extinction Radiative Extinction

label: Factor of safety
text: If confirmed for more materials, NASA may need to add a factor of safety to 1-g flammability limits.
quote: If proven for more materials, this may indicate the need to include a factor of safety on 1g flammability limits.

label: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
text: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is the main method used to assess flammability of materials for habitable U.S. spacecraft.
quote: NASA STD 6001 Test 1 is the major method used to assess flammability of materials intended for use in habitable environments of U.S. spacecraft.

label: Test 1 is pass/fail
text: Test 1 is a pass/fail upward flame-propagation test run in the most severe oxygen and pressure environment expected in the spacecraft.
quote: The method is a pass/fail upward flame propagation test conducted in the most severe flaming combustion environment (oxygen concentration, pressure) expected in the spacecraft

label: Range of survivable g
text: For Mylar, there appears to be a range of gravity levels within which a flame can survive.
quote: There appears to be a range of g-levels within which a flame can survive.

label: Caveat: sparse data
text: With so few data points, the exact shapes of these flammability curves and their minimums are not known.
quote: Given the sparcity of points, the exact shapes of the curves are not known, nor are the absolute minimums.

label: ISS atmosphere
text: The Space Shuttle and ISS have operated at sea-level conditions: air with 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen at 14.7 psia.
quote: the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station (ISS) have operated at normal sea-level conditions (air, 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen by volume at 14.7 psia total pressure)

label: ISS pre-breathe
text: Spacecraft materials are tested at ISS's most severe environment: 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia, the pre-breathe atmosphere for spacewalks.
quote: currently 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia which is the pre-breath environment on the ISS for spacewalks

label: Lower pressure, more O2
text: Lowering cabin pressure while holding oxygen partial pressure constant raises oxygen concentration, which increases material flammability.
quote: Keeping oxygen partial pressure constant while reducing total pressure has the effect of increasing the concentration of oxygen which in turn leads to increased flammability of materials.

label: Apollo 1 lesson
text: A major lesson of the Apollo 1 fire: it is impossible to eliminate all ignition sources.
quote: One of the major lessons learned from the Apollo 1 fire is that it is impossible to eliminate all ignition sources

label: Spacecraft ventilation
text: 30 cm/s is a reasonable maximum local spacecraft ventilation velocity.
quote: with a concurrent flow of 30 cm/s, which is a reasonable maximum local spacecraft ventilation velocity

label: Little partial-g data (1999)
text: Very few studies had experimentally treated gravity as a variable for flame spread in purely buoyant flow.
quote: However, very few have considered (especially experimentally) purely-buoyant flow influences, using gravity as a variable.

label: Reduced-gravity aircraft
text: Reduced-gravity aircraft can simulate partial gravity; a special device was developed to improve that simulated environment.
quote: A significant aspect of the experimental effort is to use a special device to improve the simulated partial-gravity environment achievable aboard reduced-gravity aircraft facilities.

label: U-shaped boundary (KC-135 data)
text: Flight data show the downward-spread flammability boundary versus gravity is U-shaped: residence-time extinction at high g, radiative-loss extinction at low g.
quote: The downward spreading boundary is U-shaped showing the dual extinction limits (insufficient residence time in high g, radiative loss in low g) now predicted by several diffusion flame models.

label: Parabolic flight (KC-135)
text: NASA's KC-135 parabolic aircraft provided partial-gravity environments of 0.1, 0.16 and 0.38 g for flame spread tests.
quote: Flight tests were performed onboard the NASA KC-135 aircraft providing partial-gravity environments of 0.1, 0.16, and 0.38 g/gEarth.

label: 1-g screening
text: NASA relies on a 1-g screening test; a material that passes is considered safe for spaceflight.
quote: NASA relies on a 1-g test for screening material flammability for flight. If a material passes this test, then it is considered safe for spaceflight.

label: 1 g may not be the worst case
text: Microgravity research suggests normal gravity may not be the most flammable condition for a material.
quote: However, microgravity research has suggested that normal gravity may not represent the most flammable condition for a material.

label: Burns at 0 g or lunar g, not 1 g
text: Some materials that will not burn at 1 g will burn at 0 g with a low-speed flow, or at partial gravity such as lunar.
quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).

label: Near the most flammable condition
text: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.
quote: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.

label: Quenching and blowoff branches
text: NASA's flammability boundary (after T'ien 1986) has a quenching branch and a blowoff branch, plotted against gravity level or characteristic flow speed.
quote: Flammability Boundary Quenching Branch Blowoff Branch % O2 Flame No Flame 1-g Studies Gravity Level (g/gEarth) or Characteristic Flow Speed (cm/s)

label: 34% O2 + lunar g
text: 34% oxygen combined with lunar gravity could be quite challenging for fire safety.
quote: 34% + Lunar-g could be quite challenging from the point of view of fire safety.

label: Fire on the Moon (FM2 concept)
text: NASA Glenn proposed a small chamber to conduct the first-ever combustion tests on another world.
quote: We propose to use a small chamber to conduct the first-ever combustion tests on another world.

label: Official knowledge gap (2021)
text: A 2021 NASA exploration-atmospheres decision memo names material flammability in low and partial gravity a significant knowledge gap.
quote: Identifies material flammability in low- and partial-gravity at these conditions to be a significant knowledge gap for exploration

label: NRC decadal survey
text: The 2011 NRC decadal survey made fire-safety research on flammability screening and suppression one of its highest-priority enabling recommendations.
quote: One of the highest-priority enabling recommendations made in Chapter 9: Applied Physical Sciences in Space was “Fire safety research to improve methods for screening materials for flammability and fire suppression in space environments.

label: Lunar buoyant flow
text: Scaling: a small burning sample with about 100 cm/s buoyant flow on Earth would have about 40 cm/s on the Moon.
quote: if a small (1-cm), engulfed, burning sample on Earth has U1 ≈100 cm/s, then on the Moon the same sample would have U1 ≈40 cm/s

label: Artemis 3 cabin atmosphere
text: Large-scale fire-growth tests were run to inform the choice of cabin atmosphere for the Artemis 3 mission.
quote: Large-scale fire growth tests were performed to inform the decision regarding cabin atmosphere for the Artemis 3 mission

label: Conservatism varies
text: How conservative Test 1 is varies with material and cannot be determined from the test data.
quote: The degree of conservatism varies with material and cannot be determined from the test data

label: Depends on flow
text: Whether Test 1 is conservative may depend on the flow velocity and direction chosen for the comparison.
quote: The question of conservatism of Test 1 therefore may rest on the determination of velocity and flow direction at which to compare

label: Thin high-O2 database
text: Test 1 is run at the atmosphere of use, but its database is smaller at higher oxygen concentrations.
quote: Test 1 is run at atmosphere of use, though data base is smaller at higher oxygen concentrations.

label: Skylab and Apollo atmospheres
text: Exploration cabins may use enriched-oxygen, low-pressure atmospheres, as Skylab (70% oxygen, 5 psia) and Apollo (100% oxygen, 5 psia) did.
quote: Exploration environments may have an enriched oxygen, low pressure atmosphere. • Skylab 70% oxygen, 5 psia • Apollo 100 % oxygen, 5 psia

label: Smoldering not tested
text: Smoldering combustion is not covered by NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
quote: Smoldering not covered under NASA Std. 6001, Test 1.

label: Most stringent at 1 g
text: Test 1 is an upward flammability test, considered the most stringent test in normal gravity.
quote: NASA STD 6001, Test 1 is an upward flammability test, considered the most stringent test in normal gravity.
